band.text:
Schools and local groups visit several times a year, and a visit is prepared the week before by
pulling a small selection of robust, vivid material onto a table in the workroom rather than taking a
party into the strong room. Children handle facsimiles and look at originals. The selection is
different each time, chosen for the group, and returned to the shelves the same afternoon with the
strong room log completed as usual, school visit or no school visit, and the log initialled by both
volunteers.

Volunteers on the desk keep a running list of the questions they could not answer, with the
researcher's name and what was tried, and the list is read at each committee meeting. It is the
archive's best measure of what it lacks. A question that comes up three times in a year usually
means either that a collection is uncatalogued and therefore invisible, or that the town once had a
record it no longer has and the archive should be asking around for it before the last person who
remembers it is gone. It is also, quietly, the archive's whole collecting policy.

Requests to reproduce an image in print or online go to the committee with the reference number
and the intended use, and permission is given freely to anyone who credits the archive and refused
to anyone who will not. There is no fee for private or educational use and a modest one for
commercial use, set each year and printed on the request form. The point of the fee is not income. It
is that a publisher who has paid for an image tends to caption it correctly and to send the archive a
copy of the book, and both of those things matter more than the money. The credit line is printed on
the request form too, and the committee checks each spring that it was used.

provenance.key:
what is most asked for and most fragile, not around what is easiest to feed through the machine,
which is usually the least wanted material in the room and the least likely to be asked for.

Scans are made at the resolution written on the card by the scanner, saved in the uncompressed
master format, and named by reference number followed by a sequence number. A derived copy at
reading size is made for the catalogue. The master is never edited, cropped or rotated after capture;
if it is wrong, it is rescanned. Corrections to a master are the digital equivalent of writing on the
original and are treated with exactly the same seriousness by everyone, without exception.

Masters are kept in three places: on the workroom computer, on the external disk in the strong
room safe, and on the disk that the treasurer keeps at home. The two disks are swapped on the first
Saturday of the month at the same time as the water alarm is tested, and the swap is signed on the
same sheet, by the same hand, at the same time. Storage that lives in a single place is not storage but
a hope, and the archive lost the whole of its first year of scanning in 2009 by hoping rather than
checking.

The annual report is one side of paper and is read aloud at the town meeting in March. It states how
many accessions arrived, how many boxes were catalogued, how many visitors and enquiries were
served, what was digitised, and what went wrong. The last item is the one people remember and
the one the committee is most tempted to soften. It is left as written, because a report that admits
no failures is not believed about its successes either, and it should not be.

Finally, the notes themselves. They are revised every few years by whoever is doing the most work
at the time, and each revision is dated and kept, so that a future volunteer can see not only what the
rules are but how they came to be. A rule that nobody can explain is a rule that will be quietly
dropped, and most of the rules here were paid for by a loss that somebody once had to stand up and
explain to the town, in person, at the meeting in March, when the report was read aloud.
